title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
extended_summary:
This report examines how generative AI can be integrated into secondary school instruction when teachers act as co-design partners rather than passive adopters. The core questions are how teachers design and implement AI-assisted tools in regular classrooms, how teacher judgment and AI competency shape student-AI interactions and instructional outcomes, and what support conditions enable effective classroom use. The study is framed as an early-stage classroom pilot of AI as a "third agent" that can support inquiry, formative feedback, and instructional decision-making while teachers retain authority.

The intervention was the Colleague AI Classroom platform, which included four features: Teaching Aide for structured student-AI conversations, Assessment with AI Feedback/Grading, AI Tutor for student help-seeking, and Student Growth Insights for summarizing student interaction patterns. Over a seven-week professional learning and implementation arc, teachers attended weekly meetings, planned AI-integrated lessons, implemented activities in live classes, and provided reflections through surveys, forms, interviews, meetings, and platform logs. The design combined qualitative feedback with quantitative descriptive usage and survey data.

Participants were 21 in-service teachers and more than 600 students in grades 6-12 across four Washington State public school districts and one independent school. The contexts were regular synchronous classrooms spanning math, science, ELA, social studies, and other subjects. Teachers designed the activities and students used the platform during class, with participation voluntary and non-AI parallel versions available. The study therefore reflects teacher-mediated classroom integration rather than student-directed independent use.

The main conclusions are that generative AI showed promise when tightly scaffolded by teachers, aligned to instructional goals, and used primarily for formative purposes. Teachers reported that AI could support student inquiry, personalized feedback, revision, and instructional adjustments, but effectiveness depended heavily on teacher framing, prior AI experience, interface usability, and subject/grade-level fit. The report emphasizes that AI worked best as a teaching partner rather than a replacement, with teachers retaining evaluative authority and mediating trust, interpretation, and personalization. The findings are explicitly exploratory and limited by geography, self-report, lack of direct observation, and use of a single platform.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory co-design pilot using teacher surveys, reflections, interviews, and platform logs, with no randomized or quasi-experimental comparison and no direct validated student outcome analysis. It provides useful implementation evidence but only limited causal credibility.
impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest promising but unclear impact: teacher-reported benefits for engagement, inquiry, and efficiency are positive, but effects are descriptive, mixed across contexts, and not supported by causal effect sizes or standardized achievement outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-mediated classroom use of a generative AI platform ('Teaching Aide' and 'AI Tutor') to support student inquiry, discussion, brainstorming, and guided academic help in grades 6-12 across subjects.
AI-assisted rubric generation, automated grading, and narrative formative feedback on student work, with teachers reviewing and retaining final grading authority.
Student Growth Insights aggregates patterns from student-AI interactions to surface misconceptions, common questions, and progress indicators for teachers' instructional adjustments.

finding.finding_summary: The pilot reported strong descriptive evidence that the platform reduced teacher workload in feedback and monitoring workflows. Across 58 assessments in 33 classrooms, median AI grading coverage was 92.2%, suggesting high automation of first-pass scoring/feedback, and teachers reported faster turnaround for personalized feedback and lower oversight burden via conversation summaries and Student Growth Insights. No causal estimate or standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Platform usage logs (AI grading coverage, submission/resubmission rates), teacher survey/reflection reports on feedback turnaround and monitoring burden
finding.study_size: 21 teachers; >600 students overall; 58 assessments across 33 classrooms; 936 student submissions
finding.std_deviation: Submission rate SD=27.9%; other SD not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Teachers generally reported improved student engagement with AI-supported classroom conversations when activities were well scaffolded: 28% of implementations were rated as showing thoughtful engagement, 66% mixed engagement, and 6% limited engagement. Teachers also described increased confidence and lower-pressure participation for some students, especially multilingual learners, but these findings are perception-based and varied substantially by subject, grade band, and implementation quality.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported engagement ratings and qualitative reflections on confidence/participation
finding.study_size: 18 teachers reporting on Teaching Aide implementations; up to 600 students in 21 classrooms

finding.finding_summary: The report suggests AI-supported conversations and feedback may promote inquiry, revision, self-improvement behavior, and evidence-based reasoning when teachers provide strong framing, but outcomes were inconsistent across contexts. For Teaching Aide, 35% of teacher-reported sessions said the tool helped most students learn, 62% said some students learned, and 3% said none benefited; however, these are descriptive teacher judgments rather than direct performance measures.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported learning benefit, observations of revision behavior, inquiry depth, and reasoning during AI-supported tasks
finding.study_size: 18 teachers for Teaching Aide learning reports; >600 students overall

finding.finding_summary: ELA-related results were described as promising but uneven. High school English teachers reportedly used AI for prewriting and brainstorming that improved essay quality, and some students used AI feedback to revise writing, but the report provides no direct literacy test scores, writing rubric gains, or effect sizes, and notes weaker ELA engagement patterns than in some other subjects.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on writing quality, brainstorming/prewriting support, and AI-assisted revision
finding.study_size: ELA teachers/classes included within 21 teachers and >600 students overall; exact ELA n not_reported
